subject: Chemistry
description: Ionic, covalent, metallic, hydrogen bond, polar/non-polar, VSEPR, exam-favourite contrasts

questions.stem: A bond formed by complete TRANSFER of electrons from one atom to another is called:
questions.explanation: Ionic bond — electron transfer; usually between a metal (low ionisation energy → loses e⁻) and a non-metal (high electron affinity → gains e⁻). NaCl: Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8); Cl (2,8,7) → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Strong electrostatic attraction. Properties: high m.p./b.p., crystalline solids, soluble in polar solvents (water), conduct electricity in molten/aqueous state. Covalent — sharing of electrons. Metallic — 'sea' of delocalised electrons among metal cations. Hydrogen bond — weak attraction between H (bonded to N/O/F) and a lone pair on another N/O/F.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: In the water molecule (H₂O), the bond between H and O is:

options.option_text: Polar covalent (electrons shared but unequally — O is more electronegative)

questions.explanation: H-O bond — polar covalent. Electronegativity: O (3.44) > H (2.20); ΔEN ≈ 1.24 → covalent with significant polarity (dipole, δ⁺ on H, δ⁻ on O). Pauling rule of thumb: ΔEN > 1.7 = mostly ionic; 0.4-1.7 = polar covalent; <0.4 = non-polar covalent. Water's polarity → universal solvent for ionic and polar molecules; high boiling point (100 °C) due to extensive H-bonding; ice less dense than liquid water (open H-bond cage). H₂O molecule shape — bent (V-shaped), 104.5° due to two lone pairs on O; sp³ hybridisation.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The shape of the methane (CH₄) molecule is:
questions.explanation: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) — pairs around central atom arrange to minimise repulsion. CH₄: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral, 109.5°. Common shapes by AXₙEₘ (A=central, X=bond, E=lone pair): AX₂ → linear (CO₂, 180°); AX₃ → trigonal planar (BF₃, 120°); AX₂E → bent (SO₂, ~120°); AX₄ → tetrahedral (CH₄, 109.5°); AX₃E → trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, ~107°); AX₂E₂ → bent (H₂O, ~104.5°); AX₅ → trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅); AX₆ → octahedral (SF₆, 90°). Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs → compress bond angles.

questions.stem: Hydrogen bonding is responsible for the unusually HIGH boiling point of:

options.option_text: Water (compared to H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te which are heavier but boil far lower)

questions.explanation: Water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C — anomalously high for its molar mass (18 g/mol). Compare: H₂S (34 g/mol) boils at −60 °C; H₂Se −41 °C; H₂Te −2 °C. Reason — water has extensive H-bonding between molecules (H bonded to highly electronegative O can form H-bond with another O's lone pair). Each water molecule can form up to 4 H-bonds. Other consequences of H-bonding in water: ice is less dense than liquid water (life in lakes survives winter); high specific heat (climate moderation); high surface tension; capillary action (xylem in plants). HF, NH₃, alcohols, carboxylic acids, DNA base pairs — also exhibit H-bonding. Methane / ethane / He — only weak London dispersion forces; very low b.p.

questions.stem: Metals are good conductors of electricity because:

options.option_text: Metal atoms are charged ions in fixed positions
They have a 'sea' of delocalised valence electrons that can flow freely under an applied potential

questions.explanation: Metallic bond model: lattice of positive metal cations in a 'sea' of free / delocalised valence electrons. Properties explained: ELECTRICAL conductivity (electrons drift); THERMAL conductivity (free electrons + lattice vibrations carry heat); MALLEABILITY + ductility (layers slide without breaking the bonding); LUSTRE (free electrons absorb + re-emit visible light); high m.p. (strong bond) — though not always (Hg is liquid at RT). Best conductors: Ag > Cu > Au > Al > Fe. Copper used in wiring (cheaper than Ag), Al for overhead transmission (lighter), Au for fine electronics (no oxide layer).

questions.stem: A coordinate (dative) bond is one where:

options.option_text: Both atoms equally share the electrons
Both shared electrons come from the SAME atom (the donor) — e.g., NH₄⁺ formation

questions.explanation: Coordinate / dative covalent bond — once formed, indistinguishable from a regular covalent bond, but its origin is one-sided. Examples: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ (nitrogen donates its lone pair to the proton); H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺ (hydronium); CO molecule has one σ + one π + one dative bond (one of the bonds in C≡O is a dative bond from O to C). Key in coordination chemistry — ligands donate lone pairs to a central metal ion forming complex compounds (e.g., [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ in K₄[Fe(CN)₆]). Werner won the Nobel 1913 for coordination chemistry.

questions.stem: Among CO₂, H₂O, NH₃, BF₃ — which has a NET ZERO dipole moment despite having polar bonds?

options.option_text: CO₂ and BF₃ (both have symmetric geometries that cancel out the bond dipoles)

questions.explanation: Dipole moment depends on both bond polarity AND molecular shape. CO₂ — linear, two C=O bonds in opposite directions cancel → μ = 0 (despite polar bonds). BF₃ — trigonal planar, three B-F dipoles at 120° vector-sum to zero → μ = 0. H₂O — bent (104.5°), two O-H dipoles add up to give a net dipole (μ ≈ 1.85 D). NH₃ — trigonal pyramidal, three N-H dipoles + lone pair give net dipole (μ ≈ 1.47 D). Symmetric molecules (CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, SF₆, CCl₄) — zero dipole moment. Asymmetric (H₂O, NH₃, CHCl₃) — non-zero dipole.
